For people with no dengue history planning short trips, vaccination may be considered from age 4 based on risk-benefit. Dengue remains one of the fastest-growing infections globally, with about 100 million symptomatic cases annually; Australian cases are almost entirely overseas infections. Australians frequently travel to Indonesia, Thailand, India, Vietnam, and Fiji. Symptoms include high fever, headache, chills, swollen lymph nodes, muscle/joint pain, fatigue, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and a pink rash. In Australia, dengue infections peaked in 2024 at 2,381 and fell to 1,863 in 2025. Qdenga is a two-dose (0.5 mL) vaccine given 12 weeks apart, with full protection after completion.

Pneumonic plague, caused by Yersinia pestis, is the most dangerous form and is the only form transmitted between people via respiratory droplets. Symptoms can begin within about 24 hours and include fever, chills, headache, malaise, cough and shortness of breath; without treatment, death can occur within 18–24 hours, though antibiotics with early diagnosis can save lives. articleSummary: Pneumonic plague is the rarest, most dangerous form of plague caused by Yersinia pestis, infecting the lungs and spreading via respiratory droplets. It can be primary (inhaled from an infected person or animal) or secondary (from another plague focus). Transmission requires close contact. Symptoms include sudden fever, chills, headache, cough with sputum, shortness of breath and chest pain; incubation is hours to three days with rapid deterioration. Without timely antibiotics, death can occur within 24 hours of onset. Early diagnosis and treatment markedly improve survival. First-line antibiotics are streptomycin or gentamicin; doxycycline or fluoroquinolones are alternatives; therapy lasts at least seven days, with isolation for 48 hours after starting treatment. Mortality without treatment approaches 100%; with timely treatment around 17% (2020 meta-analysis). Endemic regions include Africa (DRC, Madagascar), parts of Asia and the Americas; in U.S., Southwest (NM, AZ, CA, CO). A case in Irkutsk, Siberia, underscores lab risk.

articleSummary: Kenya records its first Ebola death after a Kenyan man who had lived in the DRC fell ill there, then traveled by road to Uganda and flew from Kampala to Nairobi on October 3. Officials should publish updates on the 28 contacts, explain airport passages, and fight rumours during the 21-day monitoring period.

articleHeadlineTranslated: How dangerous is pneumonic plague, and can it be treated?

articleSummary: Pneumonic plague, caused by Yersinia pestis, remains an active global hazard, not a relic of medieval times. Unlike bubonic plague, pneumonic form spreads via airborne droplets and can arise as primary pulmonary infection or as a complication of bubonic/septicemic plague. Incubation is one to several days; early symptoms mimic severe respiratory illness—high fever, headache, malaise, chest pain, fast breathing, cough with or without bloody sputum—and can progress rapidly to death within days without treatment. Today treated with common antibiotics; early diagnosis and immediate therapy dramatically improve outcomes. If diagnosed, patient isolation and prophylactic antibiotics for close contacts are advised. The disease persists in natural foci worldwide, including Africa (DRC and Madagascar), Asia, and the Americas; Russia’s Siberia and Altai have long-standing circulation. A cross-border natural focus between Russia and Mongolia was confirmed in August 2026, with monitoring through 2029, highlighting ongoing risk.
